A B S T R A C T
The existing studies mainly focused on the cascading failure of the whole metro but rarely on stations. In this
paper, we map a metro station into a directed and hierarchical network, and propose a cascading overload failure
model to study the network dynamic vulnerability. The passenger behavior and node load update are considered
based on impedance function and mutual flow redistribution. Without changing the network topology, a flow
optimization strategy is proposed to improve the network performance against cascading failure. Yuantong
station of Nanjing Metro is studied. The results show the network is vulnerable and global failure occurs easily
under small node tolerance. When the node tolerance excesses a critical value, the network can transit abruptly
from global failure to balance state. We obtain that the critical node tolerances are 0.17 for the largest degree-
based attack(LDA) and 0.19 for the largest load-based attack(LLA). The ranges of the optimal flow redistribution
coefficient are identified by the flow optimization strategy, which are [0.15 0.2] for LDA and [0.2 0.25] for LLA.
The result indicates that a proper guidance of passenger flow can be beneficial to the network performance while
a strong intervention to passenger flow can instead increase the cascading failure risk.
1. Introduction
Many cities in the world have large and complex metros. Taking
China as an example, Beijing, Shanghai, and Nanjing metros all have
dozens of lines and more than one hundred of stations [1]. Most metro
stations are limited and crowded underground infrastructure. There may
be a small portion is aboveground, but the space is also limited. With the
increase of metro size and passenger demand, the stations become more
and more large and complex. Stations are the passenger gathering and
switching center. In a station, there are usually many facilities with
complex layout and connection. When passengers enter and exit a sta­
tion, they need to pass through facilities with multi-layer spatial dis­
tribution characteristics. During this process, the failure of any facility
service can affect the passenger flow distribution of the entire station,
thereby affecting station operation. In a metro, stations are connected by
lines and closely related with each other by train dispatch. Therefore, as
the basic operating unit, the stability of stations is crucial for the reliable
operation of the entire metro network.
However, most studies treated stations as single nodes and focused
on the vulnerability and reliability of the whole metro network
composed of these nodes [2,3]. An important reason is that the topology
of metro networks is relatively clearly and there is several efficient to­
pology representation methods, such as L-space, P-space, and B-space
[4]. This provides convenience for studying the vulnerability of metros
at the network level, and L-space is widely used because it realistically
reflects the real topological structure of the metro network. Based on
L-space representation and complex networks, many researchers have
studied the topological vulnerability of metros with various topology
indexes [2,5,6]. These studies are usually static and cannot reveal the
dynamic impacts on passenger flow and network performance under
accidents. Some studies of dynamic vulnerability can overcome these
limitations of topological studies, such as the impacts of passenger de­
mand, route choice, and operation capacity on the vulnerability of metro
or rail transit network [7–9]. It is worth noting that the capacity of nodes
in a functional system is limited, nodes may be in failure as the load
exceeds the node capacity. Moreover, this process can be repeated in the
system duo to new overloading induced by flow redistribution and other
coupling relationships, which is called as cascading failure [3,10] and
has received many interests in metro networks recently but is still rarely
studied for a single metro station.

In terms of structure, flow or function, a metro station also has
typical network characteristics. Passenger flow and metro lines are
dynamically interacted at stations by various facilities such as entrance,
automatic fare gate (AFG), staircase, etc. These facilities are chained
with each other by passenger flow, called as “service chain” [11]. High
density of passenger flow on the “service chain” has become a common
phenomenon in many large stations, especially during peak hours.
Although some station incidents can be predicted and possible effect can
be estimated, accidents are often unavoidable [12]. If one of the facil­
ities in the “service chain” encounters an accident such as overloading,
malfunction, and attacks, the “service chain” may be disruptive and
unable to provide normal service. For example, passengers cannot pass
through a malfunctioning or extremely congested(blocked) facility
smoothly [13]. In this case, the service ability of the facility decreases
greatly or is out of function [12], and the facility can be regarded to be in
failure for simplicity. However, when one or a few facilities fail, the
whole flow in a station will be inevitably changed, especially in peak
hours that the facilities are almost in a saturated condition. This is
because passengers always attempt to arrive at exits or platforms in a
station as fast as possible, and the flow directed to the failure facilities
will be redistributed to other normal facilities. The flow redistribution
will lead to high flow pressure to other normal facilities and cause
continuous occurrence of new overloading. It can be seen that the dy­
namic flow redistribution between facilities can trigger a cascading ef­
fect, leading to the result that some or all facilities fail in the station.
The cascading failure of facilities may cause serious impacts to sta­
tions, such as long stopping time of trains, large number of stranded
passengers, and pathway blocking. For example, In Nanjing, China, on 2
may 2019, an AFG failure occurred at some stations during the morning
peak hour, causing serious congestion and denied entering and exiting of
stations for passengers. Since the cascading failure of the facilities in a
station can bring great inconvenience to passengers and high risk to the
station security and stability, it is significant to develop corresponding
models and analyze the dynamic network vulnerability.
However, the existing works mainly focused on the cascading failure
of the whole metro network, such as network topology evolution process
[14–16], impact on passenger flow [17,18], critical attack strength [17,
19], etc. Since the structure, flow, and node organization pattern of a
station are different from the whole metro network, there are still
several research gaps that should be addressed for a single metro station.
(1) Lack of a reasonable network expression model of a metro station
based on the “service chain”. (2) On the basis of the network expression
model, there is a lack of flow redistribution methods and corresponding
cascading failure models that are suitable for station structure and can
consider flow constraints and passenger behavior. (3) It is also necessary
to consider optimizing the allocation of passenger flow at facility level
without changing the network topology and facility capacity, which is a
potential method for improving network performance with low cost. In
order to address the above gaps, we try to abstract the facilities that are
distributed on the “service chain” into a directed and hierarchical
network. Based on the network model, we consider the choice behavior
of passengers under failure and use mutual flow redistribution between
facilities to develop a cascading failure model. We also define suitable
indexes to measure the network vulnerability and propose a flow opti­
mization strategy to improve the network performance without chang­
ing the network topology. Moreover, we apply our proposed approach to
a real case to verify its effectiveness.
2. Literature review
The traffic function of a station depends greatly on its capacity. In
recent years, many valuable methods of calculation and evaluation of
station capacity have been introduced. These methods can be roughly
divided into analytical methods, simulation methods, and other dy­
namic methods. For the analytical methods, the input parameters are
relatively simple [20], such as train frequencies, average durations, and
time intervals. The analytical methods can preliminarily and fast eval­
uate the station bottleneck and capacity of different conceptual designs
by mathematical expressions. The simulation methods mainly depend
on the simulation of passenger motions with specific models or tools,
including macroscopic methods and microscopic methods. The macro­
scopic methods usually consider passengers as a continuum, such as
network flow models [21], cell transmission models [22], and the
models based on Petri-nets [23]. The microscopic methods commonly
focus on simulating individual behaviors, such as activity-based model
[24], social force-based model [25], and cellular automata [26]. The
simulation methods can evaluate the station capacity for different sce­
narios, but they usually require a large amount of pre-processed data.
Moreover, the complexity of modeling and time-consuming simulation
also need be considered. Other dynamic methods, such as queuing
theory models [27,28], stochastic model [29], graph coloring-based
approach [20], etc., have also been proposed to deeply reveal the dy­
namics of the traffic systems. Additionally, automatic fare collection
data and overloading concept have been used to evaluate station usage
and capacity [30,31]. Accurate calculation of the whole station capacity
can provide significant references for station operation. However, a
metro station is also a complex system. When travelling in the station,
passengers would be affected by many factors such as the layout of fa­
cilities, location, and station capacity. Therefore, the capacity limit of a
station or a single facility does not necessarily represent the vulnera­
bility of the whole station. It is necessary to consider the dynamic
interaction of passenger flow and the facilities when studying the station
vulnerability. The above studies mainly focus on the capacity calcula­
tion but less on the network model and corresponding dynamic
vulnerability and reliability analysis.
In recent years, the vulnerability and reliability of traffic networks
have received many attentions. The related studies include network
failure cause and effect, structure and system vulnerability, evaluation
methods, and so on. These studies have been deeply discussed in two
review papers [2,3]. In these studies, graph theory and complex network
analysis method have been widely used. With the advanced data
acquisition technologies, such as Automatic Fare Collection system
(AFCs) and visual sensing, the subway passenger flows can be obtained
and deeply analyzed. Some properties of passenger flows such as the
scale-free and non-equilibrium spatiotemporal distribution have been
found [32,33]. Researchers have carried out vulnerability analysis
considering passenger flow. Xiao et al. found that the heterogeneity and
vulnerability of the Beijing subway network vary over time when
considering passenger flow [34]. Zhang et al. proposed an improved
double-weighted vulnerability analysis model, and addressed the most
vulnerable subway stations, sections, and lines [35]. Zhang et al.
analyzed the vulnerability of London subway stations based on historical
events and demographic passenger demand, and showed that the
vulnerability of subway stations depends on location, topology and
other characteristics [36]. Pan et al. gave a specific definition of elas­
ticity and vulnerability from the perspective of supply and demand of
transportation system. They analyzed and summarized relevant in­
dicators and research methods in detail from qualitative and quantita­
tive perspectives, and clarified the importance of graph theory in
analysis [37]. In addition, some researchers introduced system dynamics
method for vulnerability and reliability analysis. Chen et al. proposed a
hybrid method combined with system dynamics and Monte Carlo
simulation to evaluate the vulnerability of subway system operation
from a long-term perspective [38]. Researchers have deeply studied the
influence of network structure and passenger flow on network vulner­
ability and reliability. However, metro belongs to a dynamic network
with passenger flow [39]. Local failure can spread in metro duo to the
coupling between stations, which leads to the change of topology and
flow and affects the dynamic vulnerability of the network.
Cascading failure analysis is an effective way to study the network
dynamic vulnerability because it can clearly reveal the dynamic failure
spreading process of real systems. In recent years, the vulnerability

assessment based on cascading failure has received increasing interest
for traffic networks and many methods have been proposed, such as the
Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) epidemic model [40], the ma­
chine learning [41], and the disaster spreading theory [42]. Based on the
representation of metros with complex network or graph theory, the
Coupled Map Lattices (CMLs) and load model have been widely applied.
CMLs can map the dynamic behavior of real systems into coupling
equations conveniently and realize the full coupling of different network
information. Based on CMLs, the cascading failure of urban rail transit
network [14,43], road traffic network [44], and multi-layer rail transit
network [45] were analyzed. The influences of CMLs parameters have
been studied and the results showed that larger perturbation and
coupling strength can lead to higher probability of network failure.
Some researchers have revised the conventional CMLs to consider more
network information and characteristics. Shen et al. proposed a
bi-directional coupled map lattice model to consider the direction of
sectional flow in metro and used it to study the cascading failure of
Nanjing metro network. They optimized the network robustness by a
traffic redistribution model with adjustable parameters [16]. Zhang
et al. proposed an integrated coupled map lattices (ICML) based on
passenger flow redistribution rules addressing in-flow and out-flow
passengers at stations, and studied the vulnerability of weighted urban
rail transit networks subjected to the external perturbation [19]. Lu et al.
proposed an improved CMLs model to address the evolution process of
cascading failures on rail transit network. They found that the propa­
gation of network cascading failure depends on the station’s anti-risk
ability, geographical location, and type of adjacent stations [15].
Zhang et al. extended CMLs to multimodal public transit system(MPTS)
and quantified bus route service disruptions under interdependent
cascading failures. They studied Nanjing’s MPTS to verify the adapt­
ability of the proposed model and gain insights to guide operation
management [46]. However, the CMLs-based models depend greatly on
the initial node states and the practical meaning of some abstract model
parameters, such as perturbation and coupling strength still needs to be
further studied. Differently, load model can directly consider the rela­
tionship between network flow and node capacity, which makes it more
close to the reality. Based on load model, Goldbeck et al. developed an
integrated, dynamic modeling and simulation framework and used it to
study the resilience of the electricity distribution and London metro
against failure propagation [47]. Ma et al. constructed an evaluation
indicator system for rail transport network vulnerability and simulate
the cascading failure process of Xi’an rail transit network using a load
capacity model [48]. Yin et al. established a multi-layer directed
weighted (time) network of urban rail transit network and conducted
cascading failure analysis on passenger travel [18]. Some researchers
considered the dynamic and fluctuating characteristics of flow in met­
ros. Shen et al. proposed a cascading failure model by load matching and
studied the failure propagation of Nanjing metro under load fluctuation
[16]. Zhang and Thomas Ng simulated the propagation of cascading
failure through a linear threshold (LT) load model, and studied the dy­
namic network robustness against the fluctuation of passenger
flow-induced cascading failures under different failure modes [49]. In
these studies, the relationship between network flow and node states
were deeply discussed under different scenarios and some effective
protection methods such as node or edge protection and robust station
capacity assignments have been proposed.
It can be seen from the above literature review that the existing
studies mainly concentrated on the whole metro topology but focused
less on stations. The stations are the interaction centres between a metro
and the external passenger flow. Their stability can directly affect the
traffic performance of the whole metro. In fact, a metro station is also a
complex system composed of many facilities. An unexpected accident in
a station can cause the chain failure of the facilities duo to the interac­
tion of passenger flow and facilities, which greatly influences the secu­
rity of the station. Therefore, it is significant to develop the
corresponding models and analyze the system dynamic vulnerability.
However, the existing cascading failure models for the whole metro
network are unsuitable for a single station. The reasons are as follows.
First, the structure and flow of a station is different from the whole metro
network. In a metro, all the stations (nodes) are the origins and desti­
nations of passengers and passengers can enter or leave the network at
any node. In a station, the origin or destinations of passengers are en­
trances (exits) or platforms, and the passenger flow has different di­
rections. For a non-transfer station, the flow has two opposite directions,
i.e., form platform to exit and form entrance to platform. While for a
transfer station that connects at least two lines, there is transfer pas­
senger flow between lines. Moreover, different directions of passenger
flows can be influenced by many factors, such as the passenger behavior
and facility layout, which may lead to a more complex failure spreading
process. Second, the node organization pattern is different from the
whole metro network. In a metro, the nodes are equivalently distributed
according to their geographical locations and organized by the flow
relationships established by lines. In a station, the passengers pass
through different facilities such as AFG, stairs, and escalators, which are
hierarchically distributed on passenger paths and interacted with each
other by passenger flow. It can be seen passengers receive the service
from a series of the facilities with strong interrelation with each other in
a metro station. Therefore, when studying the failure spreading process
and dynamic vulnerability of the station, we not only should consider
nodes and their connections but also should consider the layered service
structure on passenger paths.
In this paper, we map the facilities and passenger flow of a station
into a directed and hierarchical network, and propose a cascading fail­
ure model to study the network dynamic vulnerability. The main works
of this paper are as follows. (1)A facility network model is constructed
based on the passenger flow and facility layout. The network model is
directed and hierarchical, which can accurately describe the structural
characteristic of a metro station and the complex interaction process
between facilities and passenger flow. (2)A cascading failure model of
the facility network is proposed. In the model, the choice behavior of
passengers is considered by an impedance function and the node load is
updated by mutual flow redistribution between facility node layers. (3)
Without changing the network topology, a flow optimization strategy is
proposed to improve the network performance on resisting cascading
failure. The strategy can realize different flow control patterns conve­
niently from pure passenger behavior-based movement to homogeneous
flow redistribution. (4) Yuantong station of Nanjing Metro is studied as a
real case. The facility network vulnerability, the critical node tolerance
for limiting failure propagation, and the optimal flow redistribution for
improving network performance, are obtained. The results verify the
reasonability and effectiveness of the proposed models.
This paper provides an approach for the model and analysis of the
vulnerability of station facility network under cascading overload fail­
ure and theoretical supports for the emergency flow management in
metro station.
3. Facility network of a metro station
3.1. Network structure
In a metro station, the passenger flow can be roughly divided into
three distinctive categories, i.e. the ingress passenger flow(from the
entrances to the platforms), the egress passenger flow(from the plat­
forms to the exits), and the transfer passenger flow(from the platforms of
a line to the platforms of another line) [11]. A transfer station is the
station that connects at least two lines. In each category of passenger
flow, passengers should pass through different facilities to arrive at the
platforms or exits, such as Ticket Vending Machine(TVM), Automatic
Fare Gate(AFG), Staircase, and so on. This can be regarded as a “service
chain” that describes the gathering and distributing process of passen­
gers, and the passengers in the “service chain” receive specific services
from a series of facilities. It can be seen the “service chain” is composed

In the “service chain”, each service can be provided by one or several
facilities. Based on complex network, we can regard them as the nodes in
the same node layer and denote the passenger flows between the nodes
in different node layers by directed and weighted edges. Then, a station
can be mapped into a hierarchical network with a certain number of
service layers, and there are usually several nodes in each layer. It is
noted different stations may have different structures. For illustration
purpose, we show a simple network model in Fig. 2.
As Fig. 2 shows, the nodes are divided into different layers according
to their locations and functions on the passenger paths. The directed
edges represent the passenger flow between nodes. We can see from
Fig. 2 that the facilities form directed paths for the passengers. Some
links between the inner layers are usually separated with each other for
smooth evacuation of passenger flow. For example, one channel is for
passengers to enter, and the other channel is for passengers to leave.
However, the passenger flows of different directions still have certain
relationship between them because they are intersected with each other
in some public areas. The impact of this relationship on the dynamic
vulnerability and cascading failures can be roughly considered by the
flow redistribution between edges and the failure of the corresponding
nodes connecting multiple directions. In addition, there are usually
multiple entrances or exits in a station, which can make some passenger
flows intersected with each other. The passenger flows also can be
influenced by the layout of the nodes such as elevator, stairs, adver­
tisements, shops. Duo to the complex layout and limited space, there
may be a certain correlation between the passenger flows. For example,
flow collision between different passenger flows may occur in the station
hall. However, this correlation has great uncertainty since it can be
influenced by many factors, such as the passenger flow volume, pas­
senger walking speed, station structure and space, etc. For the sake of
simple calculation and studying the general pattern of the failure
spreading process, we assume these flows are independent of each other
and represent them by directed and weighted edges in this study. In
addition, the impact of the relative position of nodes on passenger flow
can be preliminarily considered through the flow redistribution, walking
distance, and corresponding impedance function of passenger behavior.

When passengers enter a station, the flow and node information
usually can be acquired in a short time. Therefore, it is reasonable to
assume that passengers can make decisions on which node to select with
the knowledge of the network information. The user-equilibrium (UE)
model [50] is based on the fact that passengers select a path for mini­
mizing their cost and the selection on the individual level can lead to the
flow equilibrium on the whole network. The UE model has become a
widely-accepted and efficient method for traffic flow assignment, and it
can be solved by the classic Frank-Wolfe algorithm [51]. However, for
the algorithm, variable demand and large network size will lead to the
fast growth of computational complexity and decrease of accuracy. In
this study, we can utilize the network characteristics to improve the
calculation efficiency and accuracy. In addition, before cascading failure
is triggered, the initial state of a functional system should be in a balance
state [52]. For a metro station, it describes the initial network state that
the input flow and output flow is balanced by successful passenger de­
livery and no facility node is in overload failure. In this case, the OD
demand between entrances and platforms is relatively steady. Therefore,
we can assign the initial passenger flow from a static view to improve the

5. Cascading overload failure model
5.1. Cascading process
In real networks, node failure may trigger continuous failure to other
nodes through coupling relationships. The failure will propagate with
time until the entire network is stable or finally collapsed, leading to a
shift degradation of network performance called ‘cascading failure’. A
metro station is also a complex system composed of various facilities.
These facilities form a “service chain” and provide multiple paths for
passengers to reach their destinations. The passenger motional charac­
teristics are closely related to the layout of the facilities. When a local
failure is triggered in the network, passengers will attempt to select
other paths. This will increase the load on other normal facilities. If the
inflow volume excesses the maximum capacity of the facilities, over­
loading failure will occur. Furthermore, the failure will radiate along the
“service chain” until the stations can no longer maintain any type of
passenger flow if there is a continuous overloading. It can be seen the
intrinsic mechanism of the cascading failure is the propagation of fa­
cility overload failure induced by the passenger behavior based-flow
redistribution along the “service chain”.
In this section, we propose a model to simulate the cascading failure
process of the facility network of a metro station based on the network
structure and flow. In terms of node failure, the conventional flow
redistribution is to directly redistribute the flow of the failure nodes to
other adjacent nodes. However, this flow redistribution is unsuitable for

7. Conclusions and discussions
A metro station usually consists of many facilities that are distributed
on the passenger paths between platforms and entrances (exits). The
failure of one or several facilities can easily lead to the failure of other
facilities duo to the flow interaction between them, and the intrinsic
mechanism is the propagation of facility overload failure induced by the
passenger behavior based-flow redistribution along the “service chain”.
In this paper, we map a station into a directed and hierarchical network
and propose a cascading failure model to study the network dynamic
vulnerability. Furthermore, without changing the network topology, a
flow optimization strategy is proposed to improve the network perfor­
mance resisting cascading failure. The facility network model can cap­
ture the structural characteristic of metro station and the complex
interaction process between facilities and passenger flow. The cascading
failure model considers the choice behavior of passengers by an
impedance function and clearly describes the destructive process of fa­
cilities based on mutual flow redistribution between facility layers. The
flow optimization strategy can simulate different flow control patterns
conveniently from pure passenger behavior-based movement to homo­
geneous flow redistribution. which is of low cost and can fast respond to
the failure spreading. The proposed method is applied to Yuantong
station of Nanjing Metro, quantifying the vulnerability of the station
under cascading failure and identifying the critical node tolerance for
limiting failure propagation and the optimal flow redistribution coeffi­
cient for improving network performance.
Based on the simulations, we obtain the following conclusions. First,
smaller node tolerance can lead to faster decrease of the network
vulnerability indexes and global failure. This means the facility redun­
dancy is important to the station performance, and the network is very
vulnerable under small facility redundancy. Moreover, for the same
node tolerance, the network failure spreads faster under LLA than that
under LDA. Second, we find the network can transit abruptly from global
failure to balance network state that many facilities can alive when the
node tolerance is larger than a critical value αc. This provides a reference
for resisting failure spreading by optimizing the facility capacity. Since
smaller αc usually corresponds to lower cost, it is meaningful for station
modifying and design. We obtain αc = 0.17 for LDA and αc = 0.19 for
LLA under the passenger behavior-based flow redistribution. However,
changing the facility capacity is not flexible for the current passenger
flow. By flow optimization, we obtain the optimal flow redistribution
coefficient ηopt ∈[0.15 0.2] for LDA and ηopt ∈[0.2 0.25] for LLA. The
corresponding optimal acs are 0.15 for LDA and 0.17 for LLA, which are
smaller than those without optimization. The result indicates that a
proper guidance of control of passenger flow can be beneficial to the
network performance resisting cascading failure while a strong inter­
vention of passenger flow can instead increase the risk of cascading
failure. In real application, we can roughly redistribute ηopt percentage
of the passenger flow of the failed nodes to other normal edges homo­
geneously to achieve the flow optimization effect.
This paper provides a theoretical approach for the dynamic vulner­
ability assessment and flow optimization of a metro station under
cascading failure. There are still some limitations of this paper that need
to be studied. First, the network model and flow redistribution are still
primitive. It is necessary to consider the interaction of passenger flows
and the uncertain correlation between the flows in the same and
different directions. Second, other network information, such as the type
of timetable, train route frequencies, and heterogeneity of the traffic
(also known as the “traffic mix”), can be used to model more practical
passenger behavior. Finally, various scenarios such as dynamic
incoming and outgoing passengers, facility recovery, and multiple initial
failures need to be studied.
